lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: Welcome to Web APIs and Real-Time. In this course we're going to answer a question that sounds simple and turns out to have a lot of layers: how does a server tell a browser that something just happened? Think about a live cricket or football scoreboard. A goal goes in, and within a second every person watching sees the number change without touching refresh. By the end of this course you'll know exactly how that works, and more importantly, you'll know what each approach costs you, so you can choose on purpose instead of copying whatever a tutorial used.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: Here's the project. We're going to build a live match scoreboard. There's a small Node server, built with Express, that holds a single object called `matchState`. It has the home team, the away team, the two scores, and the match clock. There's also a little simulator that changes that state every few seconds, so goals and fouls keep happening while we work. And there's a plain HTML page, `scoreboard.html`, with a script called `scoreboard.js` that needs to keep the numbers on screen current.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: The interesting part is that we will deliver those updates to the browser four different ways. First, short polling, where the page just asks again and again. Second, long-polling, where the server holds the question open until it has an answer. Third, Server-Sent Events, which is a one-way stream over normal HTTP. And fourth, WebSockets, a full-duplex connection that starts life as an HTTP request and then switches protocols. Same scoreboard, same data, four transports. That's the best way I know to feel the differences.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: The course has five parts. We start with HTTP and polling, so you understand why plain request and response can't push anything. Then we cross the boundary into WebSockets by studying the Upgrade handshake and what frames look like on the wire. After that we compare the transports properly, with real measurements of bytes, latency and open connections. Then we deal with the part most tutorials skip, which is resilience: reconnecting with backoff, heartbeats, and backpressure. We finish by shipping the scoreboard with one transport per feature.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: What do you need coming in? Basic JavaScript, and you should be comfortable running a Node script from a terminal. You don't need to know anything about sockets. I'll show code as I type it, I'll explain why before how, and whenever something feels like magic I'll open the browser dev tools and show you the actual bytes. If you're following along, create a folder called `scoreboard`, run `npm init -y`, and install Express and a package called `ws`. We'll use `ws` later, but it's nice to have it ready.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: Let's set up the starting point so the next lecture begins with something running. Create `server.js`. We require Express, create the app, and serve a static folder called `public`. Then we define `matchState` as a plain object with `home: 'Mumbai'`, `away: 'Chennai'`, `homeScore: 0`, `awayScore: 0` and `minute: 0`. We also add a number called `version`, starting at zero, which goes up every time anything changes. Remember that `version` field. It looks like a small detail now, but in the polling and long-polling lectures it's going to be the hero.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: Finally the simulator. I'll write a `setInterval` that runs every three seconds. Inside it we bump `minute`, and with some random chance we add a goal to one of the teams. Every time we change anything we also do `matchState.version += 1`. Then we call `app.listen(3000)`. Start it with `node server.js`, and you should see the server listening. Nothing visible yet, but the state is changing in the background. In the next lecture we'll look at what the browser is actually allowed to do with HTTP, because that decides everything that follows.

Before we make the scoreboard live, we need to be precise about what HTTP actually promises, because every real-time technique we'll use is a workaround for one specific limitation. HTTP is a request and response protocol. The client speaks first. The server answers. And then, as far as the protocol is concerned, the conversation is over. The server has no way of saying, out of the blue, hey browser, someone just scored. It can only reply to a question that was already asked.

Let's make that concrete in our project. In `server.js` I'll add a route: `app.get('/api/score', (req, res) => res.json(matchState))`. Start the server and open `http://localhost:3000/api/score` in the browser. You get the JSON. Wait a few seconds, and you see the same page. Now refresh, and the minute has moved. The server's state changed in between, but the browser had no idea until we asked again. That is the whole problem in one picture. I'd encourage you to do this yourself rather than just watch, because seeing the stale page next to the fresh JSON makes the limitation stick.

Open the Network tab in dev tools and click on that request. Look at what's in it. There's a method, GET, a path, and a pile of request headers like `Host`, `Accept` and `User-Agent`. The response has a status line, `200 OK`, headers such as `Content-Type: application/json`, and then the body. Notice the headers are plain text and they're sent every single time. Hold that thought, because later when we measure cost, those repeated headers are going to matter a lot.

There's another thing about the contract. HTTP is stateless. Each request stands on its own, and the server isn't required to remember the previous one. That's great for scaling, because any server in a pool can answer any request. But it also means that when we say we want the server to push, there is no built-in notion of a client the server can push to. It has no list of who's listening. We'll have to invent that, either by keeping connections open or by keeping our own list.

So what are our options, given the contract? One, the client asks repeatedly, which is polling. Two, the client asks, and the server deliberately delays the answer, which is long-polling. Three, the server answers once but never finishes the response, streaming data as it goes, which is how Server-Sent Events work. Four, we ask HTTP to stop being HTTP on this connection and switch to something bidirectional, which is the WebSocket upgrade. Every technique in this course is one of those four moves.

One more detail worth knowing is that modern HTTP, versions 1.1, 2 and 3, all keep this same request and response model at the application level. HTTP/2 lets you multiplex many requests on one connection and has a feature called server push, but that was meant for sending assets early and browsers have largely removed it. It is not a general way to send live data to a page. So don't expect the newer version of HTTP to rescue us here.

Let's write down the model we'll use for the rest of this course. The client initiates, the server responds, and any liveness has to be either simulated by the client asking often, or by the server stretching out its response. In the next lecture we do the simplest possible version of that: we ask often. We'll write the polling loop in `scoreboard.js`, watch it work, and then watch it waste a surprising amount of effort.

Let's make the scoreboard actually update. The simplest idea is the one everyone reaches for first: ask the server every second. This is called short polling. Open `public/scoreboard.js`. We write an async function called `fetchScore`. Inside, we do `const res = await fetch('/api/score')`, then `const state = await res.json()`, and we call a function `render(state)` that writes the team names and the scores into the DOM. Nothing special. Then at the bottom we write `setInterval(fetchScore, 1000)`.

Open the page, and it works. Numbers tick, goals appear within a second or so. For a first version, that's honestly fine, and I want you to respect that. A lot of production dashboards run on exactly this. It's simple, it works through every proxy and firewall, it needs no special server code, and it's easy to debug because each poll is just a normal request you can see in the Network tab. That matters, because the best technique is the simplest one that meets your requirements, and we should know exactly when it stops meeting them.

But now look at that Network tab while the page is open for a minute. Sixty requests. Now ask yourself how many of them carried new information. The simulator changes things every three seconds and goals are rare, so most of those responses are identical to the one before. We are sending a full request, with all its headers, and receiving a full JSON body, just to be told nothing changed. Multiply that by ten thousand viewers and your server is handling ten thousand requests per second for a scoreboard that changes once every few seconds.

We can already reduce the waste a little using our `version` number. Change the fetch to `/api/score?since=${lastVersion}`. On the server, if `req.query.since` equals the current `version`, we respond with `res.status(204).end()`, meaning no content. The browser still makes the trip, but the response is tiny. In `scoreboard.js` we only call `render` if the status is 200, and we store the new version. You've saved bandwidth, but you haven't saved the requests themselves, and you haven't saved any server work per request. This is a cheap trick, and it's worth having in your toolbox even if you never move beyond polling.

Now the other side of the trade. Updates are late by up to the polling interval. With a one-second interval, a goal can show up anywhere from zero to one second after it happened, so on average half a second late. If you drop the interval to 100 milliseconds to feel more live, you multiply the request load by ten. That's the fundamental tension in short polling: freshness and cost are tied together, and you can only buy one with the other.

So where does short polling make sense? When updates are infrequent and delay is acceptable, like checking whether a long export job has finished, or refreshing a dashboard every thirty seconds. Where it hurts is anything that wants to feel instant. Try this as a small experiment: set the interval to 200 milliseconds, open the page in five tabs, and watch the server's request log fly. In the next lecture we fix the waste in a smarter way, by making the server hold the request instead of answering instantly.

Long-polling keeps the polling idea but flips who waits. Instead of the client asking every second and mostly hearing "nothing new", the client asks once, and the server holds that request open until it actually has something to say. When there's an update, the server answers. The client immediately asks again. From the browser's point of view it's still plain HTTP, but updates now arrive the moment they happen, not on the next tick of a timer.

Let's build it. In `server.js` we need somewhere to park the waiting requests. I'll declare `const waiting = []` near the top. Then add a route, `app.get('/poll', ...)`. Inside, read `const since = Number(req.query.since)`. If `matchState.version` is already greater than `since`, we answer right away with `res.json(matchState)`, because the client is behind and should catch up. Otherwise we push the response object into `waiting`, and we don't call `res.json` yet. The request just sits there.

Now we need to release them. Wherever the simulator changes state, after we bump `version`, we add a loop: `while (waiting.length) { waiting.pop().json(matchState) }`. All the parked requests finally get the new state. But there's one more thing we need, a timeout, because proxies and browsers don't like requests that never finish. So when we park a response, we also start a timer with `setTimeout`, say 25 seconds, and when it fires we remove the response from `waiting` and send `res.status(204).end()`. The client treats a 204 as "nothing yet, ask again".

Now the client. In `scoreboard.js` we replace the interval with a loop. I'll write `async function poll() { while (true) { ... } }`. Inside, we try `fetch('/poll?since=' + lastVersion)`. If the status is 200, we parse the JSON, render, and update `lastVersion`. If it's 204, we just continue and ask again. And in a `catch`, we wait a second before retrying so a dead server doesn't make us spin in a tight loop. Notice there's no timer for freshness anymore. The loop is the heartbeat.

Run it. Open the Network tab and you'll see something different: a single request sitting in the pending state, sometimes for twenty seconds. Then a goal happens, the request completes in a flash, and a new one starts. Updates now show up essentially the instant the server has them. That's a big improvement over short polling, and it's why long-polling powered a whole generation of chat apps and notification systems before WebSockets existed. Keep that picture in your head, because it's the mental model for everything else in this chapter.

But be honest about what's still happening. Every update costs a complete HTTP response and a new request, with all the headers again. Between the response arriving and the next request landing there's a small gap where the server has no parked request for that client, and updates in that gap have to be caught by that `since` version check. That's why the version number matters so much: without it you'd lose events in the gap. We'll come back to these costs with real numbers. First, though, let's look at what a truly persistent connection looks like, starting with the header that makes the switch happen.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: We've seen how far plain HTTP can be stretched. Now let's look at the mechanism that lets us leave it behind, because the WebSocket protocol doesn't start from nothing. It starts as an ordinary HTTP request, and the header that turns it into something else is called Upgrade. In this lecture we'll learn what that header means in HTTP itself, which is bigger than WebSockets, and then we'll watch it in our scoreboard. Think of this lecture as the doorway between the first chapter of the course and everything that follows, so it's worth getting the picture crisp.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: HTTP/1.1 has a general feature: a client can send a request that includes `Connection: Upgrade` and an `Upgrade` header naming a protocol it would like to speak instead. The server has three choices. It can ignore the header and answer normally. It can refuse. Or it can reply with the status `101 Switching Protocols`, and from that point on the very same TCP connection stops carrying HTTP and carries whatever protocol was agreed. WebSocket is the most famous user of this, but the mechanism is generic.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: Why does it work this way, instead of WebSockets just opening a fresh connection on a new port? Because of the real world. Port 80 and port 443 are open almost everywhere. Corporate firewalls, hotel Wi-Fi, mobile carriers, they all let HTTP traffic through. If WebSockets had required a new port, a huge fraction of users simply couldn't connect. Starting as HTTP means the connection passes through the same infrastructure, reuses existing cookies and authentication, and goes through the same TLS setup as any other secure request.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: Let's see it with our own eyes, without any browser. In the terminal I'll run curl against a server that doesn't understand WebSockets yet, our existing Express app. The command is `curl -i -H "Connection: Upgrade" -H "Upgrade: websocket" http://localhost:3000/`. The `-i` flag shows the response headers. Our server just ignores the upgrade request and replies `200 OK` with the HTML page. That's the first choice I mentioned: a server that doesn't know the protocol answers as if the header wasn't there.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: That detail is actually important for design. An upgrade is a request, not a command. The client is asking, and any server along the path is allowed to say no. This is also why, when you debug a WebSocket that mysteriously fails to connect, the first question is always whether something in the middle, like a load balancer, an nginx config or a corporate proxy, stripped or rejected those two headers. We'll see a lot of failures that look like WebSocket bugs but are really Upgrade failures.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: Now let's prepare the server side for the next lecture. In `server.js` I'll change how we start things. Instead of calling `app.listen` and discarding the result, we write `const server = app.listen(3000)`, keeping the HTTP server object. That object emits an event called `upgrade` whenever a client sends an Upgrade request. I'll add `server.on('upgrade', (req, socket, head) => { console.log('upgrade asked for', req.headers.upgrade) })`. Notice that the `socket` is the raw TCP socket. We are below Express now, before any response object exists.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: Start the server again and rerun that curl command. This time you'll see our log line print `upgrade asked for websocket`, and the curl hangs, because we received the upgrade request and haven't answered it. That's exactly the gap we're going to fill in the next lecture, where we write the handshake response by hand. It's a good one to do manually once, because after that you'll never wonder what the `ws` library is hiding from you.

So let's talk about what actually happens at the start of a WebSocket connection. I'll explain it first and then we'll write the server side of it by hand in `server.js`. A WebSocket connection begins with something called the handshake, and it starts as a regular HTTP request. The browser sends a GET request to the server but includes a special header: Upgrade: websocket. It also includes a Sec-WebSocket-Key header which is a randomly generated base64-encoded value. The browser is essentially asking the server to upgrade this HTTP connection to a persistent WebSocket connection. This is why WebSocket URLs start with ws:// or wss:// but the initial handshake itself travels over HTTP.

Let's see that in the browser, because it's much clearer when you can look at it. In the page's console I'll type `new WebSocket('ws://localhost:3000/live')`. It will fail, since our server doesn't answer the handshake yet, but that's useful: open the Network tab, filter by WS, and click the failed request. You'll see the request headers exactly as described. `Connection: Upgrade`, `Upgrade: websocket`, `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13`, and the `Sec-WebSocket-Key`, which looks like twenty-four characters of random base64. Version 13 is the version everybody uses, so you can treat that header as a constant.

Now the server's turn. Here is the part that people find mysterious, so I'll go slowly. When the server receives the upgrade request it responds with HTTP 101 Switching Protocols. It takes the client's Sec-WebSocket-Key, concatenates a fixed GUID string to it, hashes the result with SHA-1, and base64 encodes it. This becomes the Sec-WebSocket-Accept response header. The client verifies this value to confirm it is talking to a genuine WebSocket server and not a misconfigured proxy. Once the 101 response is received, the HTTP connection is upgraded and both sides can now send frames in either direction at any time without the request-response overhead of HTTP.

Let me say why that exchange exists at all, since it feels like an odd dance. The key and accept values are not security in the sense of authentication or encryption. Their job is to prove that the server really understood the WebSocket protocol, and that this isn't a cached or confused HTTP response being mistaken for one. That's all it proves. It also stops a normal web page from tricking a non-WebSocket server into acting like one, because a page can't control those headers freely.

Okay, now we write it. In `server.js` we require the `crypto` module. The fixed GUID is the string `258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11`, and it's defined in the protocol specification, RFC 6455, so don't try to change it. In our `upgrade` handler we read `const key = req.headers['sec-websocket-key']`. Then `const accept = crypto.createHash('sha1').update(key + GUID).digest('base64')`. That one line is the entire trick: concatenate, SHA-1, base64. You can find the same constant in every language's WebSocket library, which is a nice sanity check that we're not making anything up here.

Then we write the response straight onto the socket. I'll call `socket.write` with a string made of the status line `HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols`, then `Upgrade: websocket`, then `Connection: Upgrade`, then `Sec-WebSocket-Accept:` followed by our `accept` value, and finally an empty line, meaning a carriage return and line feed twice at the end. That blank line matters. Without it the browser keeps waiting for more headers. Now try the same `new WebSocket` call in the console again.

This time the Network tab shows a status of 101, and the console shows no error. We have a connection. And here's the moment I want you to think about: what happens next. After the WebSocket handshake completes, the connection becomes a full-duplex channel. Unlike HTTP where the client must always initiate a request, with WebSocket the server can push data to the client at any time. Data is sent in frames rather than complete HTTP messages, which makes it much more efficient for real-time applications like chat, live dashboards, or collaborative editing. The connection stays open until either side explicitly closes it with a close frame, or the network drops.

For now our server doesn't read or write anything after the handshake, so the connection just sits open. In the next lecture we'll look at what those frames look like on the wire, how big they are, and how to read one byte by byte. Before we move on, one reflection exercise: take the `Sec-WebSocket-Key` from your own request, compute the accept value with a small Node script, and check that it matches what our server sent.

Last lecture ended with an open connection and nothing flowing over it. Now let's look at what actually travels. After the 101 response, HTTP is finished on this socket. What we exchange are frames, and understanding the frame format is what turns WebSockets from magic into something you could implement on a weekend. We won't implement all of it, but we'll read real frames out of our scoreboard server, and I think that makes everything else feel solid.

Here's the structure, starting with the first byte. The top bit is called FIN, and it says whether this frame is the final fragment of a message. Large messages can be split across several frames, and FIN is how the receiver knows when the last piece has arrived. Then there are three reserved bits, which are zero unless an extension like compression is negotiated. And the lower four bits of that first byte are the opcode, which says what kind of frame this is.

The opcodes you need to know are short. Opcode `0x1` is a text frame, with UTF-8 payload. Opcode `0x2` is binary. Opcode `0x0` is a continuation, meaning more of the same message is coming. Then there are control frames: `0x8` is close, `0x9` is ping, and `0xA` is pong. Control frames are small, at most 125 bytes, and they can't be fragmented. Ping and pong are going to be central when we talk about heartbeats later in the course, so remember that they live at the protocol level, below your messages.

The second byte holds a bit called MASK, and then the payload length in seven bits. If the length is 125 or less, that's the length, and we're done. If it's 126, the next two bytes hold the real length as a 16-bit number. If it's 127, the next eight bytes hold it as a 64-bit number. So a tiny scoreboard update, say 40 bytes of JSON, costs just two bytes of header from the server, and six from the browser. Compare that with a few hundred bytes of HTTP headers on every poll.

Now the masking, which surprises people. Every frame that a browser sends to a server must be masked. The sender picks a random four-byte masking key, puts it in the frame, and XORs each payload byte with the key, cycling through its four bytes. Frames from server to client are not masked. Why? It isn't encryption, because the key travels right there in the frame. It exists to stop badly behaved proxies from confusing a WebSocket payload with an HTTP request, which could poison caches. The browser handles all of this for you.

Let's decode one by hand. In `server.js` inside the `upgrade` handler, after writing the 101, I'll add `socket.on('data', (buf) => { ... })`. Inside, I read `const opcode = buf[0] & 0x0f`, `const masked = (buf[1] & 0x80) !== 0`, and `let len = buf[1] & 0x7f`. For short messages the mask key is `buf.slice(2, 6)` and the payload starts at byte six. Then a loop does `payload[i] = buf[6 + i] ^ mask[i % 4]`. Convert with `toString('utf8')` and log it.

From the browser console, once the socket is open, I can call `ws.send('hello')` and our server logs `hello`. We've just parsed a real WebSocket frame by hand. It's rough, since it ignores fragmentation and large lengths, so in practice we'll hand this job to the `ws` package. But now you know what's inside it. You also now know why a WebSocket message of ten bytes is vastly cheaper than an HTTP request carrying the same ten bytes, and we'll quantify that in the next chapter.

We've been poking at WebSockets from the console. Now let's use the browser WebSocket API properly, from `scoreboard.js`, and switch our server to the `ws` package so we can stop parsing bytes. First the server. At the top of `server.js` I'll write `const { WebSocketServer } = require('ws')`. Then, instead of our hand-written upgrade handler, `const wss = new WebSocketServer({ server, path: '/live' })`. That attaches to the same HTTP server and handles the handshake we just wrote, including the key hashing and the 101 response.

Next, what the server does on a connection. `wss.on('connection', (ws) => { ws.send(JSON.stringify(matchState)) })`. Every time a client connects, we send it the current state immediately, so it never has to wait for the next goal to see a score. Then in the simulator, after we bump `version`, we loop over `wss.clients` and, for each client whose `readyState` equals `WebSocket.OPEN`, we call `client.send(JSON.stringify(matchState))`. That's our whole broadcast. Compare that with the waiting list in long-polling. There's no parked request to find and no timeout to manage.

Now the browser side, which is gloriously small. In `scoreboard.js` I'll replace the polling loop with `const socket = new WebSocket('ws://localhost:3000/live')`. When deployed over HTTPS you must use `wss://`, because browsers block insecure WebSockets from secure pages. Then we attach handlers. `socket.onopen` can just log that we connected. And `socket.onmessage = (event) => { render(JSON.parse(event.data)) }`. That's it. The `event.data` is a string for text frames, and by default a Blob for binary, which you can change using `socket.binaryType`.

Let me point out the lifecycle, because beginners trip on it. A socket has a `readyState`: 0 is CONNECTING, 1 is OPEN, 2 is CLOSING, and 3 is CLOSED. You can only call `send` when it's 1, otherwise you get an error, so if your code might send early, check the state or queue the message. The events are `open`, `message`, `error`, and `close`. Notice that `error` carries almost no detail on purpose, and the `close` event has a `code` and a `reason` that tell you more.

Let's also make it two-way, since that's the real advantage. I'll add a small button on the page called Cheer. Its click handler runs `socket.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'cheer' }))`. On the server we add `ws.on('message', (data) => { ... })`, parse it, and when the type is `cheer` we increment a counter and broadcast the new count to everybody. The client never sends a new HTTP request, and the server never needs to be asked. Open two browser windows, click Cheer in one, and watch it update in the other.

To close cleanly, call `socket.close(1000, 'done')`. Code 1000 means normal closure, and the server's `close` handler fires with that code. If the server dies or the network drops, you'll see code 1006 instead, which means the connection closed abnormally and there was no close frame. Keep that in mind, because in the resilience chapter we'll use close codes to decide whether to reconnect. For now, our scoreboard is live over a WebSocket. Next chapter, we're going to compare it against long-polling honestly, because it isn't always the right answer.

Now we have two real-time versions of the scoreboard, long-polling and WebSockets, and the obvious question is which one you should use. Let's compare them properly, starting with a short history, because it explains why long-polling exists at all. I'll keep it conceptual in this lecture, and in the lecture after next we'll measure it with our own code. By the end of it you should be able to defend your choice to a teammate, with reasons rather than habit. That's the skill I care about, more than any one API.

Rewind to the years before WebSockets were widely supported. Developers wanted chat, notifications and live feeds, and the browser offered exactly one tool: HTTP requests. So they made it work. Before WebSockets, the common trick for real-time updates was long-polling. The client sends an HTTP request and the server deliberately holds it open instead of responding immediately. When data becomes available, the server responds, and the client instantly sends another request to wait again. It simulates a push, but every message still pays the full cost of an HTTP request and response — new headers, sometimes a new TCP connection — and there is always a gap between responses where the client is reconnecting.

Let's map that onto our scoreboard code. In the long-polling version, each update meant the `/poll` response completed, the client ran `render`, and a new `fetch` started. That fetch needs headers, cookies if you have any, and potentially a fresh TCP and TLS handshake if the old connection was closed by some intermediate server. The gap I just mentioned is the time between those two. If a goal and a foul land in that gap, the server has to hold both until the next request arrives, which is exactly why we built that `version` check.

Now the other side of the comparison. A WebSocket replaces all of that with a single long-lived, full-duplex TCP connection. After the initial HTTP Upgrade handshake, both sides can send frames at any time with only a few bytes of framing overhead — no repeated headers, no reconnect gap. This makes WebSockets dramatically more efficient for high-frequency, bidirectional traffic like chat, live cursors, or trading data. Long-polling still has its place: it is simpler, works through old proxies, and is fine for low-frequency updates where a dedicated connection per client would be wasteful.

Let me give you a way to think about this that I use in real projects. Ask three questions. How often do updates happen? Do messages flow in both directions? And how many clients will be connected at the same time? A scoreboard that changes every few seconds, shown to many viewers, who never send anything back, is a one-direction low-frequency flow. A multiplayer cursor that moves sixty times a second in both directions is the opposite.

There are also practical constraints that don't show up in benchmarks. A WebSocket needs your infrastructure to support the Upgrade handshake, so load balancers need configuring for it, and sticky routing or a shared message layer becomes necessary when you run more than one server process. Long-polling is plain HTTP, so it works with anything that handles HTTP. And a held connection costs memory on the server either way, so neither is free in a big deployment. We'll look at that in a moment.

Let me also warn you about a common mistake. People hear that WebSockets are faster, and they replace everything with them, including features that are just occasional notifications. Then they own reconnect logic, heartbeats, authentication on a long-lived socket, and scaling a stateful connection layer, to deliver a message once an hour. WebSockets are the right tool when the traffic justifies the complexity. For many apps the honest answer is a simpler option, and the next lecture introduces one of them.

So here's the summary I want you to leave with. Long-polling simulates push on top of request and response, and pays per message. WebSockets give a persistent, full-duplex channel and pay mostly at connection time. Neither is better in the abstract, and the right choice depends on frequency, direction and scale. In the next lecture we meet Server-Sent Events, which sits in the middle: push from the server over ordinary HTTP, without the upgrade.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: There's a transport I deliberately left until now, because it fits between the two we've compared, and for our scoreboard it might actually be the best fit. It's called Server-Sent Events, or SSE. The idea is simple. The browser makes an ordinary HTTP GET request. The server answers with a status 200, but it never finishes the response. It keeps writing text to it, whenever it has something to say, and the browser delivers each piece to your code as an event.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: The browser gives you a built-in class for it, called `EventSource`. In `scoreboard.js` I'll write `const source = new EventSource('/events')`. Then `source.onmessage = (event) => { render(JSON.parse(event.data)) }`. There's no manual reading loop, no JSON streaming parser, and no reconnect code, because the browser handles reconnection for you. If the connection drops, `EventSource` waits a few seconds and connects again automatically. That's a lot of resilience for free. Honestly, when I first saw how little code this was, I wondered why I had ever bothered hand-rolling a long-polling loop for notification features.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: Now the server. In `server.js` we add `app.get('/events', (req, res) => { ... })`. First, headers: `res.set({ 'Content-Type': 'text/event-stream', 'Cache-Control': 'no-cache', Connection: 'keep-alive' })`, and then `res.flushHeaders()` so the browser sees the response begin right away. Then we keep a set called `sseClients`, add `res` to it, and when the request closes, via `req.on('close')`, we remove it. That mirrors the waiting list from long-polling, except we never empty it on each message. Notice also that we call `res.write` and never `res.end`, because ending the response would end the stream.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: The format on the wire is plain text, and that's the beautiful thing about it. A message is one or more lines starting with `data:`, followed by a blank line. So to send our state, we write `res.write('data: ' + JSON.stringify(matchState) + '\n\n')`. The double newline ends the message. You can also add an `id:` line, and an `event:` line to name a custom event type so you can listen with `source.addEventListener('goal', ...)` instead of `onmessage`. A line starting with a colon is a comment, which is handy as a keep-alive.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: Here's the feature that makes SSE shine for our `version` idea. If you send `id: 42` with a message, the browser remembers it. When it reconnects after a drop, it automatically sends a request header called `Last-Event-ID: 42`. On the server we read `req.headers['last-event-id']` and send anything we missed. So the same version trick we hand-built for polling is part of the protocol. You can also set the delay before reconnecting by sending a line like `retry: 3000`.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: What are the limits? SSE is one-way, server to client. If the page needs to send something, it uses a normal `fetch` POST, which is fine for a scoreboard where the only thing going up is an occasional vote. It carries text only, no binary. And on HTTP/1.1 browsers allow only about six simultaneous connections per domain, so six tabs of SSE can starve your page of requests, though HTTP/2 lifts that limit by multiplexing. Also watch out for proxies that buffer responses, which delays events until a buffer fills.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: So for the scoreboard, think about what we really need. Updates flow one way, they are small, they're occasional, and we want automatic reconnect with catch-up. SSE gives all that over plain HTTP, with no upgrade, no custom frames and less code than either of our earlier versions. It's very often the best answer for live feeds, notifications and progress bars, and I'd rather you pick it for those than reach for WebSockets by reflex. In the next lecture we measure all four honestly.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: We've been saying things like "WebSockets are more efficient" and "polling wastes requests." Today we stop asserting and start measuring. We'll build a tiny benchmark harness for the scoreboard that counts three things for each transport: bytes on the wire, latency from event to screen, and open connections on the server. The numbers won't be identical on your machine, but the shapes will be, and the shapes are what teach you. Treat this as an engineering habit, because a claim about performance that you haven't measured is really just an opinion.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: Let's start with bytes. In `server.js` I'll add a small counter object called `stats` with a field `bytesOut`, and a helper called `send(res, payload)` that adds the payload length before writing. For the HTTP-based versions I also want header cost, so I use the `Content-Length` and add an estimated header size of about 250 bytes per response. That's a conservative figure for a request and response pair with typical headers, and real apps with cookies are much bigger, often a kilobyte or more. You can adjust that header estimate and rerun, and the conclusion won't flip, which is why I'm comfortable using a rough number.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: Now run a scenario. One scoreboard update every three seconds, one minute, one client. Short polling at one request per second sends sixty responses, almost all just 204 or an unchanged state, each with its headers. Long-polling sends roughly twenty, one per update, each with headers plus a new request. SSE sends twenty tiny `data:` messages of about fifty bytes each, plus the headers once. WebSocket sends the same twenty messages with two bytes of framing each, plus the handshake once.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: When you print the totals, the ordering is very consistent. Short polling is by far the heaviest, perhaps fifteen to twenty kilobytes for that minute. Long-polling is a fraction of that, but still pays headers on every message. SSE and WebSockets are both roughly just the payload, around a kilobyte. This is where my earlier point about the header size lands: for tiny messages sent often, the HTTP envelope is bigger than the message, and persistent connections win by an order of magnitude.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: Next, latency. I'll add a `sentAt` timestamp to every message the simulator broadcasts, and in `scoreboard.js` compute `Date.now() - state.sentAt` when we render, which works since both run on my machine's clock. Short polling shows an average delay near half the interval, so about five hundred milliseconds. Long-polling, SSE and WebSockets all arrive within a few milliseconds locally. Over a real network they differ by the usual round trip, and long-polling adds another round trip whenever it has to open a new connection.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: The third measure is the one people forget: open connections and memory. Add `app.get('/stats', ...)` returning counts, with `waiting.length`, `sseClients.size` and `wss.clients.size`. Then use a small script with a loop that opens a thousand clients of one type. You'll find that a held connection is cheap in Node, a few kilobytes each, so a single process can hold tens of thousands, but short polling costs CPU instead, because every poll runs your request handler. The cost moves from memory to compute.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: So here's what the measurements tell us. Short polling spends bandwidth and CPU for freshness you may not need. Long-polling is fine for low frequency and badly shaped for high frequency. SSE and WebSockets are the efficient ones, and the deciding factor between them is direction. Do you need to send from the client constantly? Pick WebSockets. If it's mostly server push, SSE is simpler. Now we have all the data to decide. Next, we'll make whichever one we choose survive a bad network.

Welcome to the resilience chapter. Everything we've built so far works beautifully on localhost, and that is exactly the problem. Real networks drop. A phone goes into a tunnel, a laptop sleeps, a deploy restarts your server, a load balancer closes an idle connection after a minute. A live scoreboard that freezes silently when this happens is worse than one that never updated at all, because users trust the numbers. So in this chapter we make the connection keep itself alive, starting with reconnecting.

Let's see the failure first. With the WebSocket version running, stop the server in the terminal with Control C and look at the page. The socket's `onclose` fires, with code 1006, and nothing else happens. The scoreboard just sits there with stale numbers. Now restart the server, and the page is still dead, because a WebSocket object can't be reopened. A closed socket is finished. To reconnect, we have to create a brand new `WebSocket`, so we need to wrap the creation in a function we can call again.

In `scoreboard.js` I'll restructure. I write `let socket` and a function `connect()` that does `socket = new WebSocket(url)` and attaches our handlers. In `socket.onclose` we call `setTimeout(connect, 1000)`. That's a first reconnect, and it works: kill the server, restart it, and the page recovers by itself within a second. Great. But this naive version has a nasty failure mode that I want you to understand, because it has taken down real systems. Try it yourself before moving on, since the restructure is only a few lines and it makes the next steps much easier to follow.

Imagine the server is down for a minute, or the server is up but overloaded. Ten thousand clients all lose connection at the same moment, and every one retries every second. The moment the server comes back, ten thousand handshakes arrive together. That overwhelms it, it fails again, all of them disconnect again, and they all retry at the same instant again. This is called a thundering herd, and a fixed retry interval makes it worse, because the clients stay synchronized with each other.

The standard fix has two ingredients. The first is exponential backoff: after each failed attempt, wait longer than before. Something like one second, then two, then four, then eight, doubling each time, up to a maximum such as thirty seconds. The second is jitter: add randomness so the clients spread out instead of marching in lockstep. Backoff reduces the load during a long outage, and jitter prevents the retries from synchronizing in the first place.

Here's the code. I'll add `let attempts = 0` at the top. In `onclose` we compute `const base = Math.min(30000, 1000 * Math.pow(2, attempts))`, and then the delay is `Math.random() * base`, which is the technique often called full jitter. We do `attempts += 1` and `setTimeout(connect, delay)`. And in `socket.onopen` we reset with `attempts = 0`, so a healthy connection forgets its history. Without that reset, a client that reconnected successfully an hour ago would still wait thirty seconds after its next blip.

Now one more detail: reconnecting is not just opening a socket. While we were disconnected, goals may have happened. In `onopen`, our server already sends the full `matchState` as the first message, which fixes the scoreboard because we send complete state. But for event streams, such as a chat, you need to send the last version you saw, as we did with `since`, so the server can replay what you missed. So remember the rule for any live feature: the reconnect protocol is part of the design, not an afterthought. Next lecture, the harder problem: noticing a connection that died without telling you.

Last time we handled connections that close. The sneakier case is a connection that dies without closing. Think about a laptop's Wi-Fi switching off, or a phone entering a dead zone, or a router in the middle silently dropping the mapping for your connection. No FIN packet and no close frame ever arrives. As far as the browser's TCP stack knows, the connection is still open, and it can take minutes, sometimes much longer, to notice. Your scoreboard looks connected, and it's frozen.

Let me say precisely why, because it's a basic property of TCP. A TCP connection is just agreed-upon state at both ends. If one end vanishes without sending anything, the other end has no way to know until it tries to send something and doesn't get acknowledgements, and then retransmission timeouts take a long time. If nobody's sending, nobody ever finds out. So an idle connection that has quietly died is indistinguishable from an idle connection that's healthy. To tell the difference, you have to send something and expect a reply.

That's what a heartbeat is. Every so often, one side sends a small message, and the other side must answer in a short time. If the answer doesn't come, the connection is considered dead. The WebSocket protocol builds this in: remember the ping opcode, `0x9`, and the pong opcode, `0xA`. When one side receives a ping, it must reply with a pong carrying the same payload. Browsers do this automatically for you, so you never write code to answer a ping.

On the server, the `ws` library gives us what we need. Inside the `connection` handler I'll set `ws.isAlive = true`, and add `ws.on('pong', () => { ws.isAlive = true })`. Then I add a `setInterval` that runs every thirty seconds and loops over `wss.clients`. For each client, if `ws.isAlive` is false, we call `ws.terminate()`, which destroys the connection immediately. Otherwise we set `ws.isAlive = false` and call `ws.ping()`. Next round, anything that hasn't answered with a pong is dropped.

This does two useful jobs at once. It detects dead clients, so our server doesn't accumulate zombie sockets holding memory. And the traffic itself keeps the connection active, which matters because many proxies and load balancers close connections that stay silent for too long, often around sixty seconds. A ping every thirty seconds keeps those middle boxes happy. Many people only find out about this in production, when connections get dropped at suspiciously exact intervals.

Now here's the browser's blind spot. The browser WebSocket API gives your JavaScript no way to send a ping or see a pong. The browser handles protocol pings invisibly. So if you want the client to detect a dead server, you need an application-level heartbeat. I'll add it in `scoreboard.js`: the server sends `{ type: 'tick' }` messages every ten seconds, and the client keeps `lastSeen = Date.now()`. A timer checks every five seconds, and if more than twenty-five seconds passed with nothing, we call `socket.close()`, which triggers our reconnect-with-backoff path.

So now we have both directions covered. The server uses protocol pings to prune dead clients and keep proxies awake. The client uses an application-level tick to notice a silent server and reconnect. Tune the intervals to your environment, since mobile networks want longer ones to save battery. Then there's one more resilience problem that appears when connections are alive but slow, which is when the server writes faster than the client can read. That's backpressure, and it's the next lecture.

Here's a failure that doesn't involve the network dropping at all. The connection is alive and healthy, but the receiver is slower than the sender. Maybe it's a phone on a bad cellular link, or a browser tab that's busy. Our simulator sends scoreboard updates, and the `send` call returns immediately regardless. But the bytes have to go somewhere, and if the client can't take them fast enough they pile up in a buffer in memory. That pile is what backpressure is about.

Let me make it visible. I'll add a stress mode to our simulator, which broadcasts an update every ten milliseconds. On the client, I'll deliberately slow things down: in `onmessage` I run a busy loop for fifty milliseconds. Now the server produces a hundred messages per second and the client can consume twenty. The extra eighty per second have to wait. On the browser side, they queue up inside the browser's networking layer. On the server side, in `ws`, if the operating system's socket buffer is full, they queue in Node's memory.

The tool for seeing this is a property called `bufferedAmount`. On the browser WebSocket it tells you how many bytes you've passed to `send` that haven't yet been transmitted to the network. For the `ws` library on the server, the same name exists on each socket. So on the server I can log `ws.bufferedAmount` for each client in the broadcast loop. When you run the stress test you'll see it climb for the slow client and stay near zero for fast ones. If you ignore it, your Node process's memory grows steadily until it falls over.

What do we do about it? The simplest policy for a scoreboard is to skip. Before sending to a client, check `if (client.bufferedAmount > 64 * 1024) continue`. The client is behind, so we don't make it worse, and since each message carries the whole `matchState`, the next message that does get through brings them fully up to date. That's called load shedding, and it's valid whenever messages are snapshots instead of deltas, where the latest value replaces everything before it.

For event-style messages, where each one matters, such as chat lines or trades, skipping isn't acceptable. There you have a few choices. Slow down the producer, by pausing a source until the buffer drains. Queue per client with a limit, and when the limit is crossed, drop the oldest messages or disconnect the client, which forces it to reconnect and resync from a known version. Disconnecting a hopelessly slow consumer is often the right call, because one slow client shouldn't be able to consume the memory that everyone shares.

The same idea applies in the browser when you send. If your page streams large uploads or rapid cursor positions with `socket.send`, check `socket.bufferedAmount` first and hold off while it's high, using a short timer to try again. It's the browser's version of the same flow control we added on the server. And also note what's different with TCP itself: TCP has built-in flow control, but the WebSocket API doesn't expose it directly, which is why this property exists.

Let's connect the three lessons of this chapter. Reconnect with backoff and jitter so an outage doesn't become a stampede. Use heartbeats so a silent death becomes a detected one. And watch `bufferedAmount` so a slow reader can't hurt the system. Those three together are what separate a demo from something you'd put in front of real users. In the last chapter, we take everything we've built and decide, feature by feature, which transport to ship.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: For the final project step, I want to answer the question we've been circling the whole course: what do we actually ship? We have a scoreboard with four working transports. Shipping all four would be silly, so let's decide the way you'd decide at work, by going through the features of the product and picking the lightest transport that meets each need. The principle I'll use is simple: choose the simplest technology that meets the requirement, and only escalate when you can name the reason.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: Feature one is the live score and match clock, which is what the whole course started with. The data flows from server to client only. It changes every few seconds. It has to survive reconnects, and it should catch up on missed updates. That's a textbook case for Server-Sent Events. We get automatic reconnects, we get `Last-Event-ID` for catch-up, we pass through ordinary HTTP infrastructure, and we write the least code. So the scoreboard's main feed becomes `/events`.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: Feature two is match commentary, short text lines that appear as they're written by a journalist. Same shape: one direction, low frequency, important not to miss messages. Another good fit for SSE, and in fact it can share the same stream with a custom `event: commentary` type, so the page listens with `source.addEventListener('commentary', ...)`. One connection, multiple event types. There's no reason to open a second connection for this. That is a good example of not multiplying connections when one will do, because every open connection has a cost on the server and on a phone's battery.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: Feature three is the crowd reactions panel, where thousands of fans send emoji cheers in real time and everyone sees a live count. Now traffic goes both ways and it's frequent, so this is where a WebSocket pays for itself. We keep our `/live` endpoint with the heartbeats and backpressure rules from the last chapter, and use load shedding, since the count is a snapshot. A reasonable detail: the server aggregates cheers and broadcasts the totals once per second, instead of rebroadcasting every single click.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: Feature four is the admin console that edits the score. This is a rare action, only a few times in a match, sent by one trusted person. A plain `fetch` POST to `/api/score` is perfect. It's easy to authenticate, easy to retry, easy to log, and gives a clear success or error. Putting this on a socket would add complexity and give nothing. And what about long-polling and short polling? We keep short polling as a fallback for ancient environments, and a status page that refreshes every thirty seconds is a good use of it.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: Let's look at the final structure in code. `server.js` now has four things: a REST route for admin updates, an `/events` SSE endpoint, a `/live` WebSocket endpoint, and a `/health` route that a load balancer can poll. A single function called `publish(change)` updates `matchState`, bumps `version`, and fans out to SSE clients and WebSocket clients together. That's the nice thing about having built these separately: the transports became thin layers over one shared state and one shared version number.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: A few deployment notes. Behind nginx or a cloud load balancer, SSE needs response buffering turned off, and WebSockets need the Upgrade headers passed through and an idle timeout longer than your heartbeat. Use `wss://` and HTTPS everywhere. If you run more than one server process, you'll need a shared channel such as Redis pub/sub so that a change on one instance reaches clients on the others. We won't build that here, but now you know exactly which problem it solves.

So that's the course. Let's take a few minutes to pull it together, because I want you to leave with a mental map you can reuse and not just a pile of code. We started with one limitation: in HTTP, the client asks and the server answers, and the server can't speak first. Every technique we built was a different answer to that limitation, and each one had a price that we measured rather than guessed.

Short polling asks often and pays in wasted requests. Long-polling holds the request open and pays a full HTTP exchange per message, with a gap while the client reconnects. Server-Sent Events keep one response open and stream text over it, one direction, with reconnect and catch-up built into the browser. WebSockets cross the Upgrade boundary, replace HTTP with frames, and give you a full-duplex channel at the cost of owning more of the lifecycle yourself.

Let me also revisit the handshake, because it's the heart of the course. A client sends a GET with `Upgrade: websocket` and a random `Sec-WebSocket-Key`. The server answers `101 Switching Protocols` with a `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` computed by appending the protocol's fixed GUID, hashing with SHA-1, and base64 encoding. After that, frames flow, opcodes tell you what each one is, and browser frames are masked. If you can explain those three sentences to a colleague, you understand WebSockets better than most people who use them.

And the resilience chapter might be the part that serves you the longest. Exponential backoff with jitter, so a mass disconnect doesn't become a stampede. Heartbeats, because a dead connection looks identical to an idle one until you test it. And `bufferedAmount`, because a slow reader will quietly eat your memory if you let it. Whatever transport you choose in a future project, those three habits transfer directly. If you only keep one chapter's worth of notes from this course, I'd keep that one.

Where should you go from here? There are some natural next steps. Try scaling the scoreboard to two server processes and add Redis pub/sub, so you feel the multi-instance problem first-hand. Look at Socket.IO, which wraps WebSockets with rooms, acknowledgements and a long-polling fallback, and see which of the things we built by hand it does for you. Read RFC 6455, the WebSocket specification, which is surprisingly readable now that you know the vocabulary. Pick one of them and spend an evening on it, because a small experiment teaches more than any amount of reading.

Also worth exploring are the newer pieces. WebTransport, built on HTTP/3, offers multiple streams and unreliable datagrams for cases where WebSockets' single ordered stream is a bottleneck, though browser support is still developing. And if you're doing server-to-server work, look at gRPC streaming. Don't adopt them because they're new. Ask the same questions we asked all course: which direction, how often, how many clients, and what happens when the network fails. They solve real problems, but only the problems they were designed for.

One last piece of advice. Build the smallest thing that works, measure it, and let the measurements tell you when to escalate. You've now built the same feature four ways, so you won't be guessing. Take the scoreboard, give it a second sport, break the network with your browser's offline mode, and see if it recovers on its own. Thanks for working through this with me, and I'll see you in the next course.
